Q653601.summary: This life-size oak crucifix shows Christ not as a serene victor but as a man who has just died: his head sinks forward, his eyes are closed and his body sags heavily from the arms. The oldest surviving large-scale crucifix north of the Alps, it marks a profound turn in Western art toward contemplation of Christ's human suffering.
facts: Archbishop Gero, who died in 976, commissioned the work; the chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg reports that when a crack appeared in the head, Gero placed a consecrated host and a relic in it, prayed, and the crack closed.
The figure is about 1.87 metres tall, and its body is deeply hollowed out from behind, so that it weighs only about 36.5 kilograms.
The radiant gilded sunburst and marble altar surrounding it today are Baroque additions, donated in 1683 by Canon Heinrich Mering.
Long assigned to the 12th century, it was redated to Gero's time by art historians in the 1920s — a date supported by dendrochronological study in 1976.
Q653601.notes: Worklist date 960 refined to c. 965–970 (Wikipedia). The paint and gilding have been renewed (a repainting of 1904 is recorded).

cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-crucifixio.summary: Three registers tell the climax of Christ's Passion and its triumph: at the top Christ hangs on the cross between the two thieves with the Virgin and John and the soldiers; in the middle his body is taken down and laid in the tomb; at the bottom the risen Christ greets the holy women with 'Chairete' ('Rejoice'), beside the empty sepulchre. The page faces Gregory's homily on Easter.
facts: The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883 and is one of the most ambitious Byzantine manuscripts to survive from the generation after Iconoclasm.
The inscription ΧΑΙΡΕΤΕ, Christ's greeting to the women in Matthew's Gospel, is written above the risen Christ in the lowest register.
cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-crucifixio.notes: Folio derived from the Gallica image sequence (view number minus 13, halved) and checked against folios named on other Commons files of this manuscript; the Commons file name gives the Gallica view number, not the folio.

cur:manuscripts-utrecht-psalter-psalm-51.summary: In a nervous, sketchy pen drawing, the Lord appears in an oval mandorla on a hillside between two groups of seated figures, while below, a figure stands beside a flourishing olive tree and raises his hand toward him; at the left a ruler sits enthroned in a colonnaded hall among armed men. The scene illustrates the psalm's contrast between the boastful evildoer and the just man who is 'like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God'.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm with a lively pen drawing that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It has 166 pen drawings, one for each psalm and canticle; it reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times (Harley, Eadwine and Anglo-Catalan Psalters).
cur:manuscripts-utrecht-psalter-psalm-51.notes: The Commons file is a detail of the drawing. The identification of the mandorla figure as the Lord (Christ-Logos) follows the psalter's consistent iconography; the image does not show the nimbus clearly.

cur:manuscripts2-stuttgart-psalter-psalm.summary: A haloed, youthful figure with a cross-staff and a book strides through a river with his followers crowding behind him, illustrating the verse above, 'in flumine pertransibunt pede' — 'they went through the flood on foot: there did we rejoice in him'. The cross-staff marks the leader as Christ, who brings his people through the waters as at the Exodus.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts2-stuttgart-psalter-psalm.notes: Identified as Christ by the nimbus and cross-staff; the psalm refers to Israel's crossing, and the leader could also be read as the Lord of the Exodus in the person of Christ. The image is the full page; the miniature occupies only part of it.

cur:monumental-naples-baptistery-traditi.summary: Standing on a blue globe against a deep blue ground, the haloed Christ in golden robes holds out an unrolled scroll to Peter, who approaches with covered hands carrying a cross on his shoulder; a palm tree rises behind. The scroll reads DOMINUS LEGEM DAT, 'the Lord gives the law'. The opposite side, with Paul, is almost entirely lost.
facts: The baptistery of San Giovanni in Fonte beside Naples Cathedral is one of the oldest in the West; its building is dated to the 4th century, and its construction is attributed to Bishop Severus (362–408) or to later bishops.

Of the scenes once set within garlands around the dome, four survive: the Traditio Legis, the Samaritan woman with the Wedding at Cana, the Miraculous Draught (or Peter on the water), and the women at the tomb.

cur:objects2-vatican-box-cover-blind-man.summary: This small ivory panel, the sliding lid of a box, shows a bearded Christ laying his hand on the eyes of the man born blind, who stands before him with an apostle behind. Its shallow, softly modelled relief belongs to the late antique tradition of Christian ivory carving. The cover was preserved among the relics of the papal chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum in the Lateran.
facts: The Italian museum label describes it as the cover of a medical box (cassetta medica), apt for an image of Christ the healer.
The relics and reliquaries of the Sancta Sanctorum were brought to light in the early 20th century and are now displayed in the Vatican Museums.
cur:objects2-vatican-box-cover-blind-man.notes: Facts come from the Vatican Museums' gallery labels as photographed; no online object record was consulted.

walters:W.537.2R.summary: Under a tall, scalloped arch the Virgin sits frontally on a broad throne, her arms spread wide, while the Christ Child sits before her holding a book. The throne, edged with great roundels, is described by the Walters as a wheeled chariot, and the whole page is framed by columns of discs with crosses and quartered patterns in red and blue-green. This simple, powerful image opens the oldest Armenian manuscript in North America.
facts: The colophon on the next page (fol. 2v) records that Sargis the Priest completed the text in the Armenian year 415, that is AD 966.

Someone later erased 'of the Armenian era' after the date and wrote 'of our Lord', which led to the book being known as the 'Gospels of the Translators', as if it went back to the 5th-century translation.
The Walters describes it as the fifth oldest among documented Armenian Gospel Books and notes that the scribe may also have painted the miniatures.
